lesson.title: Overlay Networks: A Virtual Map on Top of the Real One
lesson.summary: An overlay network is a virtual network built on top of an existing physical network by encapsulating traffic in tunnels, letting its topology and addressing be designed independently of the underlying infrastructure.
lesson.body:
The network layer normally routes a packet based on the actual, physical or logical topology of the network beneath it: how routers are connected, what paths exist, what the IP addressing looks like at each hop. An overlay network takes a different approach. It builds a virtual network on top of that physical topology, using encapsulation, wrapping one packet inside another, so that two endpoints can exchange traffic as if they were directly connected, even when the physical path between them crosses many unrelated networks and many hops.

The mechanism itself is straightforward. An overlay endpoint takes an original packet, wraps it inside a new outer packet addressed to the other overlay endpoint, and sends it across whatever underlying network exists between them, often the public internet. The underlying, or underlay, network only ever sees the outer packet and forwards it normally, having no idea what is tunneled inside. When the outer packet arrives, the receiving endpoint strips off the outer header and delivers the original inner packet as if it had arrived directly.

A familiar example is a VPN. When someone connects their laptop to a corporate VPN, the physical path from their home internet connection to the corporate gateway might cross a home router, an ISP, several internet backbone providers, and finally the corporate network's edge, many hops with no direct relationship to the corporate LAN's addressing. The VPN tunnel hides all of that: from the laptop's perspective, and from the corporate network's perspective, it looks like the laptop is directly attached to the corporate LAN, with an address from that network's own address space, regardless of the physically circuitous path the traffic actually takes.

What makes this useful in general is that it decouples logical topology from physical topology. An overlay's addressing, isolation boundaries, and virtual topology can be designed purely around what an application or organization needs, a flat internal network, isolated tenant segments, a specific mesh of virtual links, without being constrained by how the physical infrastructure underneath happens to be wired. This general idea, tunneling to build a virtual topology independent of the physical one, is the foundation for VXLAN, a specific and heavily used overlay encapsulation standard covered next.
